WHY DO WE FEAR THE WRONG THINGS?

1 Ask a nervous passenger why they grip the armrest during take-off, and they will rarely mention statistics. Measured by distance travelled, commercial flying is one of the safest ways to get from one place to another — far safer than the car journey to the airport. Yet millions of people perceive it as more dangerous than driving, and some refuse to fly at all. This gap between the risks we face and the risks we fear is not a sign of stupidity; it reflects the way the human mind evolved to make quick decisions in a world without spreadsheets or safety reports.

2 Psychologists have long argued that we judge how likely something is by how easily examples come to mind. A plane crash is reported around the world for days, complete with vivid images of wreckage and grieving families, while the thousands of people who die on the roads each year rarely make the headlines. Because dramatic events are easy to picture, we tend to overestimate how often they happen, and to underestimate the slow, quiet dangers that never become news. Shark attacks, lightning strikes and terrorist incidents all loom far larger in the imagination than in the mortality tables.

3 Certain kinds of risk seem to trigger a particularly strong reaction. Researchers use the term ‘dread risk’ to describe low-probability events that could kill many people at once, such as a nuclear accident or a new epidemic. Such risks feel uncontrollable and unfamiliar, and people often demand far greater protection from them than from everyday hazards that, over time, claim many more lives. Control matters too: drivers tend to feel safer than passengers partly because their hands are on the wheel, even though being in charge does little to change the odds of a collision.

4 Misjudging risk is not merely an academic curiosity; it can have serious consequences. After the attacks on the United States in September 2001, many Americans chose to drive rather than fly for months afterwards. One widely cited study estimated that the extra traffic may have led to around 1,500 additional road deaths in the following year — far more than the number of people killed on board the hijacked planes themselves. By avoiding a frightening but rare danger, people unknowingly exposed themselves to a familiar and much more common one.

5 Familiarity, in fact, is one of the main reasons we underrate everyday hazards. A large share of serious accidents happen at home — on the stairs, in the kitchen or in the bathroom — yet few people think of their own house as a dangerous place. The same is true of habits such as driving while tired, eating badly or never exercising: because the harm builds up slowly and nothing bad happened yesterday, we become complacent. A risk we have survived a thousand times simply stops feeling like a risk at all.

6 Numbers, unfortunately, do not always help. Many people find probability difficult to interpret, especially when it is expressed as a percentage. A headline announcing that a medicine ‘doubles the risk’ of a side effect sounds alarming, but if the original risk was one in ten thousand, doubling it still leaves the chance extremely small. Without knowing the starting point, readers have no way of judging whether the change matters, and frightening relative figures can lead patients to abandon treatments that would actually do them good.

7 None of this means we should ignore our feelings. Our intuitive sense of danger often serves us well, warning us away from a dark alley or an unstable cliff edge long before we could calculate anything. The challenge is to recognise when instinct is likely to mislead us and to check it against the evidence. Experts suggest that presenting risks in simple terms — ‘three people in a thousand’ rather than ‘0.3%’ — can mitigate some of these biases, helping people to fear a little less of what is rare and a little more of what is common.

LANGUAGE DEVELOPMENT - Talking about risk

VOCABULARY SKILLVerb + noun collocations with risk

The noun risk combines with a fairly fixed set of verbs, and choosing the wrong one immediately sounds unnatural — we take a risk or pose a threat, but we do not ‘make a risk’ or ‘do a danger’. Learning these collocations as whole chunks will make your writing about safety, health and decision-making far more precise.

take / runa risk, a chance (neutral)
posea risk, a threat, a danger (negative)
reduce / minimisethe risk, the danger, the impact (positive)
weigh up / assessthe risks, the odds, the options (neutral)
outweighthe risks, the costs, the drawbacks (positive)
raise / increasethe risk, the likelihood, concern (negative)

WHY DO SOME PEOPLE CHASE DANGER?

1. Every year, thousands of people pay large sums of money to throw themselves out of aeroplanes, climb frozen waterfalls or ski down slopes so steep that a single mistake could be fatal. To many observers, such behaviour looks reckless, even selfish, since rescue teams and hospitals often bear the cost when things go wrong. Yet those who take part in extreme sports rarely describe themselves as careless. Instead, they talk about focus, freedom and the exhilarating sense of being completely alive — feelings they say they cannot find anywhere else in modern, comfortable life.

2. Psychologists have tried for decades to explain why some people actively seek out danger while others avoid it at all costs. One influential idea is sensation-seeking, a personality trait describing the need for new, varied and intense experiences. People who score highly on this trait tend to become bored easily and may be drawn not only to dangerous sports but also to travel, unusual food and loud music. Research suggests that the trait is partly inherited, and that it typically peaks in late adolescence before gradually declining with age.

3. However, the stereotype of the adrenaline junkie who cares nothing for safety may be misleading. Interviews with experienced mountaineers, BASE jumpers and big-wave surfers reveal people who are, if anything, obsessed with control. They study weather patterns, check equipment repeatedly and rehearse emergency procedures until they become automatic. Their preparation is meticulous precisely because they understand how little room for error there is. In their own eyes, they are not gambling with their lives but taking calculated risks, reducing the danger as far as possible before deciding whether the uncertainty that remains is acceptable.

4. Interestingly, very similar language is used by entrepreneurs. Starting a business is rarely life-threatening, but it can put savings, careers and relationships on the line, and a large proportion of new firms close within their first five years. Successful founders often insist that they are not natural gamblers. Before launching a venture, they test their ideas on small groups of customers, keep their costs low and plan what they would do if things went wrong. Like climbers, they try to limit the downside while leaving room for a potentially large reward.

5. What both groups seem to share is an unusual relationship with failure. A climber who turns back a few hundred metres from the summit, or a founder whose first company collapses, may treat the experience as useful information rather than as a disgrace. Studies of serial entrepreneurs suggest that an early setback can prove valuable, provided that people reflect honestly on what went wrong. This kind of resilience — the capacity to recover, adapt and try again — may matter far more in the long run than raw courage or talent.

6. None of this means that risk-taking is always admirable. Overconfidence has killed experienced climbers and bankrupted talented business people, and luck plays a larger role in many success stories than the winners like to admit. Still, the lives of those who deliberately court danger raise an uncomfortable question for the rest of us. In a society that increasingly tries to remove every possible hazard, we may be losing opportunities to discover what we are capable of — and to learn that most fears, once faced, are smaller than they first appeared.

GRAMMAR FOR WRITING
GRAMMARMixed and inverted conditionals

Conditionals do not always follow the neat ‘first, second, third’ patterns taught at lower levels. Mixed conditionals link a condition in one time frame to a result in another, while inverted conditionals replace if with had, should or were to create the more formal, emphatic style typical of academic and official writing.

The rules below show how to combine different time frames and how to form inverted conditionals correctly.

1. Past condition → present result: If + past perfect, would + infinitive. Use it when an earlier action (or lack of it) affects the situation now.

If she had taken out travel insurance, she wouldn’t be paying the hospital bill herself now.

2. Present condition → past result: If + past simple, would have + past participle. Use it when a permanent quality or situation explains a past event.

If he were a more cautious person, he would never have invested all his savings in one start-up.

3. Had + subject + past participle replaces if + past perfect (third or mixed conditional).

Had I known the ice was so thin, I would never have walked across the lake.

4. Should + subject + infinitive replaces if in the first conditional. It sounds formal and suggests the situation is fairly unlikely — common in instructions and notices.

Should you experience any chest pain, stop exercising immediately and inform a member of staff.

5. Were + subject + to + infinitive (or Were + subject + adjective/noun) replaces if in the second conditional.

Were the government to raise the speed limit, the number of accidents would almost certainly increase.

6. Were it not for / Had it not been for + noun = ‘if something didn’t exist / hadn’t happened’. In inverted conditionals the negative is never contracted (Hadn’t I known… ✗).

Had it not been for the safety rope, the climber would have fallen more than fifty metres.

ACADEMIC WRITINGHedging and boosting — showing how certain you are
ACADEMIC WRITING SKILLHedging and boosting

Hedging means using tentative language — may, might, tend to, appear to, is likely to, it could be argued that — so that a claim is not stated more strongly than the evidence allows. Boosting does the opposite: clearly, undoubtedly, there is strong evidence that show confidence when the evidence is solid. Good academic writers balance the two, hedging speculative ideas and boosting well-established facts.

UNHEDGED: Extreme sports are dangerous, and young people who do them are addicted to adrenaline.

HEDGED: Some extreme sports may carry a considerably higher risk of injury, and it could be argued that certain participants tend to seek out intense physical sensations.

READING PRACTICE
PART 5

Read the following text for questions 30-35.

Australia’s flying foxes are ‘curious, gentle and intelligent’ – and often misunderstood

Endangered spectacled flying foxes and vulnerable grey-headed flying foxes are ‘astonishing’ animals but misinformation is rife.

One of the most spectacular sights at Adelaide’s Womadelaide music festival is not on the official lineup. As dusk approaches, thousands of grey-headed flying foxes begin chattering and stretching their wings as they prepare to ascend from their roosts in Botanic Park and set out in search of food. “It’s an amazing sight,” says associate professor Wayne Boardman, a wildlife veterinarian and flying fox researcher at the University of Adelaide. At first a few early birds take to the skies, he says, then more and more, “diving, swooping, flapping”. “As the night sky darkens, steadily the full camp take to the air – a mass of circling, squawking bats all eager to start foraging after a day of rest.”

For many festivalgoers, the nightly fly-out ritual is their first time seeing the animals, also called megabats, up close. Boardman runs a “bat tent” near one of the main stages, kitted out with displays, videos and binoculars to educate visitors and address misconceptions about the flying foxes. “They are just astonishing animals,” he says. “The loveliness of flying foxes, their sheer beauty, astonishing biology, the amazing anatomy – it never ceases to amaze me.” Yet misinformation about the animals is rife, from well-meaning parents telling children they use sound waves to navigate (they don’t), to more sinister notions including that the animals are “pests” that “don’t belong here”. “They came of their own volition,” Boardman says. Grey-headed flying foxes first arrived in Adelaide in 2010, establishing a permanent camp on First Creek, in parklands just north of the CBD, where they have increased in number from 1,000 to about 50,000 today.

Flying foxes are nomadic, capable of travelling up to 50km at night in search of food resources such as flowering gums, figs and fruit trees. Tim Pearson, a wildlife ecologist who specialises in flying fox behaviour and communication, says the “double whammy” of destroying native forests while providing alternative food sources in farms and residential areas creates the potential for human-bat conflict and harassment, identified as a threat in recovery plans for endangered spectacled flying foxes and vulnerable grey-headed flying foxes. Populations of both species have declined in recent decades, although assessing their current status has become more challenging since the national flying fox monitoring program concluded in 2022. “The Australian attitude towards wildlife has always been positive, providing it doesn’t inconvenience you,” Pearson says. Unfortunately for flying foxes, in their case it often does.

Things have been getting better, Pearson says, but flare-ups still occur when practical concerns – about noise, the animals’ impact on fruit growers, power outages or potential disease threats – are reported in breathless terms by the media. Efforts to disperse the bats are generally counterproductive and attempts to promote empathy and coexistence have not worked. Scientists now think “normalising” flying foxes might be a way forward, depicting them as a natural part of Australian wildlife in art, photography, books, community events and education. Despite their often visible and audible presence in cities and towns, representations of flying foxes in mainstream media and popular culture remain scarce and largely negative, according to the paper published in Australian Zoologist. Pearson, a co-author of the paper, works with tame education flying foxes at a wildlife park. Once people see these cute, furry animals up close, they realise they are “curious, gentle, intelligent” with individual personalities, he says.

Doug Gimesy, a wildlife and conservation photojournalist, says bats – flying foxes and microbats – make up nearly 20% of all mammals, but “don’t get 20% of the air time”. “As a group, they’re often ignored, under-appreciated and misunderstood,” he says. “At worst they’re vilified and face a constant battle of disinformation, hate speech and are even persecuted.” Gimesy began photographing flying foxes in 2016 and has since spent more than 160 days in the field, taking thousands of images that document every aspect of their lives. Through his award-winning photographs and children’s book, Life Upside Down, Gimesy is hoping to show people how magnificent the animals are, “to get people to engage and ask questions and understand”. Two images have been important to capture and share, he says. In one, a flying fox pokes its pink tongue into a eucalyptus blossom – because people don’t realise what important pollinators they are, he says.

In the other, a pup clings to its mum as it breastfeeds in mid-flight, which usually triggers an emotional response. It’s the realization “they carry their young in flight, and they’re flying mammals”. The paper says shifting attitudes towards species such as sharks and crocodiles, once subject to widespread persecution, offer optimism that contentious issues between flying foxes and people can be managed without maligning them as a species. In Fisher reserve, in the inner Melbourne suburb of North Fitzroy, children play on the green grass as an oversized flying fox takes wing with a magpie, a squirrel glider and pink paper planes against a purple sky. The colourful mural, by Alex Sugar, is one of several depicting flying foxes alongside other Australian wildlife and quirky elements. Sugar is fond of the bats, and they became a recurrent feature in his work after their nightly flyout over the Yarra River drew his attention. “We need to highlight them more in everyday culture and the issues that they’re going through as well with their current habitat,” he says.

Phrases & Idioms Wordlist

Play with fire: To do something dangerous that is likely to cause problems for you.

Push your luck: To keep taking risks after being successful, so that you may lose what you have gained.

Throw caution to the wind: To stop being careful and do something bold or risky.

Take the plunge: To finally decide to do something important or risky after thinking about it for a long time.

Stick your neck out: To say or do something that others may criticise or that could get you into trouble.

Skate on thin ice: To be in a risky situation that could easily lead to trouble.

Bite off more than you can chew: To try to do more than you are able to manage.

Better safe than sorry: It is wiser to be careful now than to regret taking a risk later.

Nothing ventured, nothing gained: You cannot achieve anything worthwhile unless you are willing to take a risk.

Put all your eggs in one basket: To depend completely on one plan or investment, so that you could lose everything.

A leap in the dark: An action whose results cannot be known in advance.

Hedge your bets: To protect yourself by supporting more than one option, so that you do not lose everything.

Tempt fate: To do something that seems to invite bad luck or disaster.

Go out on a limb: To take a position or action that is risky and that few others support.

Against all odds: Despite seeming very unlikely to succeed.

WRITING PART 2

USEFUL LANGUAGE — Opinion essay

FunctionUseful phrases
Introducing the topicIt is often argued that… / In recent years, there has been growing concern that…
Stating your opinionI would argue that… / In my view, … / I largely agree that…
Hedging a claimIt could be argued that… / This may / tends to… / There is some evidence that…
Giving examplesFor instance, … / A case in point is… / This is particularly true of…
Conceding a pointAdmittedly, … / While it is true that…, … / That said, …
ConcludingIn conclusion, … / On balance, … / Overall, I believe that…

THE TASK

You are writing an essay for an academic audience. Write 180–200 words.

Some people believe that children today are overprotected and should be allowed to take more risks in order to learn and develop. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

PARAGRAPH PLAN

Introductionparaphrase the question + state your position clearly
Body paragraph 1main reason(s) for your view + a specific example
Body paragraph 2concede the opposing view — which risks are not acceptable?
Conclusionsummarise your position in new words; do not add new ideas

RULES for Part 2 (essay)

☐  Answer the question that is actually asked — ‘To what extent…?’ requires a clear position, not just a list of points.

☐  Aim for 180–200 words in four paragraphs; going far over or under the limit costs marks.

☐  Paraphrase the question in your introduction instead of copying it word for word.

☐  Support every main idea with a reason and a concrete example.

☐  Hedge claims you cannot prove (may, tend to, it could be argued) and boost well-established facts (clearly, there is strong evidence).

☐  Show a range of grammar — for example, a mixed or inverted conditional — and use formal linking words.

SAMPLE ANSWER

In recent years, there has been growing concern that children are being raised in an environment so carefully controlled that they rarely face any danger at all. I largely agree that young people should be given more freedom to take sensible risks, as this is likely to make them more confident and capable adults.

Firstly, it could be argued that children learn to judge danger only by experiencing it. A child who climbs a tree and slips tends to understand height and balance far better than one who has only been warned about them. Were parents to remove every challenge, children might never develop this practical judgement. Moreover, there is strong evidence that independent play builds resilience, since minor failures teach young people that setbacks can be overcome.

Admittedly, some risks are simply not worth taking. Busy roads, deep water and the darker corners of the internet present real dangers that children cannot be expected to assess alone, and adults clearly have a duty to protect them.

In conclusion, while sensible supervision remains essential, I believe that overprotection may do more harm than good. Had my own parents not let me make small mistakes, I would probably be far more anxious today.

SAMPLE ANSWER

Personally, I’m largely in favour of the idea that people should take more risks, although I’d add an important condition: the risks need to be thought through.

The main argument in favour is that growth rarely happens inside our comfort zone. Moving to a new city, changing careers or starting a business are all frightening, but they’re also how people discover what they’re capable of. A good example is my cousin, who left a stable job to open a small café. Had she stayed where she was, she’d probably still be wondering ‘what if’. On top of that, many of the inventions we rely on today exist only because someone was willing to fail in public.

On the other hand, it’s worth bearing in mind that not everyone can afford to take chances. Someone with savings and a supportive family can bounce back from a failed venture, whereas a person supporting three children may lose everything. There’s also the point that some risks — like dangerous driving — put other people in danger, not just the risk-taker.

All things considered, I’d say that people should take more calculated risks, not reckless ones. Weighing up the odds, having a back-up plan and knowing when to walk away seem to me just as important as courage.

USEFUL LANGUAGE
Giving your view:Personally, I’m largely in favour of… / I’d have to disagree with the idea that…
Arguments for:The main argument in favour is that… / One clear advantage is…
Arguments against:On the other hand, it’s worth bearing in mind that… / A major drawback is…
Giving examples:A good example is… / Take, for instance, …
Adding a point:On top of that, … / There’s also the point that…
Concluding:All things considered, I’d say that… / On balance, …

INSIDE THE LIGHTS-OUT FACTORY

1 On the outskirts of a mid-sized Japanese city stands a factory where the lights are almost never switched on. Inside, rows of robotic arms weld, lift and assemble components around the clock, while a handful of engineers monitor screens from a control room upstairs. Plants like this, sometimes called 'lights-out' factories, can run for weeks without a single person on the production floor. They are still rare, but they offer a glimpse of where manufacturing may be heading as robots are deployed in ever greater numbers across the world.

2 The appeal is easy to understand. A robot can place a microchip with a precision of a fraction of a millimetre, and it will do so in exactly the same way on its ten-thousandth attempt as on its first. It does not get bored, distracted or tired at the end of a long shift, and it never needs a holiday. For products where tiny errors are costly, such as car engines or medical devices, this consistency is arguably worth even more than speed, although robots usually offer that as well.

3 Until recently, only the largest manufacturers could afford this level of automation. Industrial robots were expensive, enormous and had to be kept in safety cages, well away from people. Today, prices have fallen sharply, and a new generation of smaller 'collaborative' robots, or cobots, can work safely alongside human staff. A family-run furniture workshop can now lease a robotic arm for a monthly fee, programme it using a tablet and move it between tasks in an afternoon, something that would have been unthinkable twenty years ago.

4 Unsurprisingly, the first jobs to be affected are those built around repetitive tasks: packing boxes, tightening the same screw, moving parts from one conveyor belt to another. In some regions, the number of people employed in these roles has dropped noticeably, even as factories produce more than ever. Economists point out that the manufacturing workforce has been shrinking for decades in many wealthy countries, but automation has accelerated the trend, and the people most affected are often those with the fewest qualifications.

5 At the same time, robots are creating jobs that barely existed a generation ago. Someone has to programme the machines, repair them when they break down and oversee entire production lines from a screen. These roles tend to be better paid and less physically demanding, but they require technical skills that many existing employees simply do not have. A growing number of companies now pay for staff to retrain, turning former machine operators into maintenance technicians and data analysts rather than replacing them.

6 Automation is also changing where things are made. For decades, manufacturers moved production to countries where labour was cheap. When robots do most of the work, however, wage differences matter far less, and factories can be built closer to their customers. Several European and American firms have brought production back home in recent years, arguing that a highly automated local plant can match the output of a much larger overseas one while cutting shipping times, transport costs and emissions.

7 Robots still have clear limits. They are excellent at doing one thing perfectly, but surprisingly poor at coping with the unexpected: a slightly bent component, an unusual order, a sudden change in design. Human workers remain far better at improvising, spotting problems and suggesting improvements. The real risk, many experts argue, is not that people will become obsolete, but that their skills will if they are not regularly updated. The factory of the future may be quieter and darker, but it is unlikely to be completely empty.

LANGUAGE DEVELOPMENT - Talking about production and efficiency

VOCABULARY SKILLVerb + noun collocations

When we describe how factories and businesses change, certain verbs combine with a small, predictable group of nouns, for example boost productivity, meet demand or phase out machinery. Learning these as fixed chunks helps you write about industry precisely and naturally, rather than relying on general verbs such as make, do or change.

boostproductivity, output, efficiency (increase)
cutcosts, waste, jobs (reduce)
streamlineprocesses, operations, production (make simpler and more efficient)
meetdemand, deadlines, targets (achieve what is needed)
phase outmachinery, jobs, older models (stop gradually)
scale upproduction, operations, manufacturing (expand)

WILL 3D PRINTING BRING FACTORIES HOME?

1. For most of the last hundred years, manufacturing followed a simple rule: the bigger the factory, the cheaper each product. Goods were made in enormous quantities in a few locations and then shipped around the world through a long and complicated supply chain of ports, warehouses and lorries. 3D printing, also known as additive manufacturing, challenges that rule. Instead of cutting or moulding material, a printer builds an object layer by layer from a digital file, which means the same machine can produce a thousand identical items or a thousand different ones at roughly the same cost per piece.

2. The technology was first used mainly by engineers and designers who needed a quick prototype to test an idea before investing in expensive tools and moulds. A model that once took weeks to make by hand could be printed overnight, examined, improved and printed again the next day. Over time, however, printers have become faster, more reliable and able to work with a far wider range of materials, from plastics and resins to metals, ceramics and even concrete. Some aerospace companies now print finished engine parts that are lighter and stronger than conventionally produced ones.

3. Perhaps the most significant change is that products can be customised for individual buyers at little extra cost. Dental clinics print crowns shaped precisely to a patient's mouth; sports brands sell running shoes with soles designed around a scan of the customer's foot; hearing-aid manufacturers have almost entirely switched to printing each device individually. Products like these were once luxury items, but on-demand production is turning them into everyday ones. For businesses serving a niche market, such as replacement parts for vintage cars, printing can make a previously unprofitable product line suddenly worthwhile.

4. Supporters argue that 3D printing could make manufacturing far more decentralised. Instead of ordering a spare part from a factory on another continent, a garage or hospital might simply download the design and print it locally. Companies would no longer need warehouses holding a huge stockpile of parts that may never be used, which would reduce waste as well as transport emissions. During recent disruptions to global shipping, small workshops printed face shields and valves for nearby hospitals within days, showing how quickly local production can respond to a crisis.

5. The picture for jobs is mixed. On the one hand, printing could displace some workers in traditional factories, as well as drivers and warehouse staff whose jobs depend on moving goods over long distances. On the other hand, it may create new opportunities close to home: designers, printer technicians, materials specialists and owners of small neighbourhood print shops. Unlike earlier waves of automation, which concentrated production in fewer, larger plants, 3D printing could spread manufacturing work across many small towns and cities rather than a handful of industrial centres.

6. Even so, mass production is not about to disappear. For simple items made in millions, such as plastic bottles or screws, traditional methods remain much faster and cheaper, and printed parts can still be less durable. Many analysts therefore expect a hybrid future, in which large factories continue to produce standard goods while local printers handle spare parts, personalised products and small batches. Whether local manufacturing becomes economically viable on a large scale will depend on cost, regulation and skills, but for the first time in a century, the most efficient factory may not need to be the biggest.

GRAMMAR FOR WRITING
GRAMMARThe passive with modals & the causative (have / get something done)

When we describe a process, we are usually more interested in what happens to the product than in who does each step, so the passive is extremely common. Modal verbs add meaning such as possibility, obligation or advice, while the causative (have / get something done) shows that we arrange for someone else to do a job for us.

The rules below explain how to form the passive after a modal verb, and when to use have or get + object + past participle.

1. Modal + be + past participle describes possibility, obligation or ability in the present or future.

The parts can be printed overnight and must be checked before they are packed.

2. Modal + have been + past participle refers to the past — often criticism, regret or deduction.

The fault should have been noticed much earlier in the process.

3. In process descriptions, the by-phrase is usually omitted because the agent is obvious or unimportant.

The metal sheets are cleaned and then cut to size (by the workers).

4. Use have + object + past participle when you arrange for someone else to do a service for you.

We had the machines serviced by an outside engineer last week.

5. Get + object + past participle means the same but is more informal, and often suggests effort or urgency.

We need to get these orders shipped by Friday.

6. The causative can also describe something unpleasant that happened to someone, usually not by choice.

The workshop had its roof damaged in last night's storm.

ACADEMIC WRITINGDescribing a process — sequencing the stages clearly
ACADEMIC WRITING SKILLDescribing a process

When you describe how something is made, the reader needs to follow each stage in the correct order. Use sequencing language such as initially, first of all, once…, after that, subsequently, at this stage, meanwhile and finally, and combine it with the passive, since the focus is on the product rather than the people.

WITHOUT SEQUENCING: The design is created on a computer. It is sent to the printer. The object is built layer by layer. It is removed and polished.

WITH SEQUENCING: Initially, the design is created on a computer. Once it has been finalised, it is sent to the printer, where the object is built layer by layer. Finally, it is removed and polished.

Combine each pair of steps into one sentence, using the sequencing word or phrase in brackets.

  1. 1  The raw cotton is collected from the fields. It is cleaned to remove seeds and dirt. (initially … then)
  2. 2  The fibres have been spun into thread. They are woven into cloth. (once)
  3. 3  The cloth is dyed. It is washed several times to fix the colour. (after that)
  4. 4  The fabric is cut into pieces. A computer checks that no material is wasted. (at this stage)
  5. 5  The pieces are sewn together by machine. The labels are printed in another part of the factory. (meanwhile)
  6. 6  The finished shirts are inspected and folded. They are packed and sent to shops. (subsequently)

Phrases & Idioms Wordlist

Run like clockwork: To operate smoothly, exactly as planned and without problems.

A well-oiled machine: An organisation or team that works very efficiently.

Up and running: Working fully; in operation after being set up or repaired.

Back to the drawing board: To start planning again because the first attempt has failed.

Cut corners: To do something cheaply, quickly or carelessly, often ignoring rules or quality.

Off the shelf: Ready-made and available immediately, not designed for a particular customer.

Made to measure: Made specially to fit or suit one particular person or purpose.

Roll off the production line: To be produced in a factory, especially in large numbers.

Grind to a halt: To slow down gradually and then stop completely.

Pull the plug on (something): To stop a project or activity, usually by withdrawing money or support.

Learn the ropes: To learn the basic skills and routines of a new job.

Get your hands dirty: To do practical, physical work rather than just giving instructions.

In the pipeline: Being planned or developed and likely to happen soon.

Iron out the kinks: To solve the small problems in a plan, product or process.

A cog in the machine: A person with a small, unimportant role in a large organisation.

PART 1.1 PRACTICE

You are a member of a local Makers' Club, a community workshop where members build and repair things. You received this email from the club's manager.

Dear Member,

I'm writing to let you know about an important change at the Makers' Club. From next month, we will be replacing half of our traditional woodworking benches with six new 3D printers and a laser cutter. We believe this will attract younger members and allow everyone to try modern manufacturing techniques. However, it does mean that there will be less space for hand tools and woodwork classes. Before we finalise the new layout, we would like to hear how you feel about this change and what training or facilities you think we should offer.

Best wishes,

The Manager

Task 1.1 — Write a letter to your friend, who is also a member of the Makers' Club. Write about your feelings about the change and what you think the club should do. Write about 50 words.

Task 1.2 — Write a letter to the manager. Write about your feelings about the change and what training or facilities you think the club should offer. Write about 120–150 words.

RULES for Task 1.2 (formal letter)

☐  Respond to the SAME message as Task 1.1 — cover the same two things (feelings + suggestions), but in more depth.

☐  Aim for 120–150 words — several short paragraphs, not one block of text.

☐  Use a formal register throughout: no contractions, slang or exclamation marks.

☐  Structure it clearly: a reason for writing, your reaction, your suggestion(s) in detail, and a polite closing.

☐  Open with Dear Sir/Madam or Dear [Title], and close with Yours faithfully/sincerely.

☐  Show a wider range of grammar than in Task 1.1 — passives with modals (could be offered, should be kept), the causative and formal linkers (furthermore, provided that, in addition).

SAMPLE ANSWER

Dear Manager,

Thank you for informing members about the planned changes to the workshop. I must admit I have mixed feelings about the news. While I am excited about the opportunity to learn 3D printing and laser cutting, I am concerned that reducing the woodworking area will discourage many long-standing members who joined the club specifically for traditional craft.

I would therefore suggest that at least a few woodworking benches should be kept, and that hand-tool classes could be offered at weekends, when demand is highest. In addition, I believe beginners' training on the new machines is essential, as most members will not have used a 3D printer before. Perhaps short evening courses could be run by experienced members.

Furthermore, it might be worth having the new equipment installed in a separate room, so that noise and dust from the woodwork area do not cause problems.

I look forward to hearing your thoughts.

Yours faithfully,

A. Karimov

SAMPLE ANSWERS

Do you enjoy making or repairing things with your hands?

Yes, to be honest, I find it really satisfying. My grandfather taught me to fix bicycles, so whenever something breaks at home, I'm usually the one who has a go at repairing it. There's nothing quite like seeing something work again because of your own effort.

Would you prefer to buy handmade or mass-produced products? Why?

It depends on what it is, really. For everyday things like phone chargers, I'd go for mass-produced items because they're cheaper and more reliable. But for gifts, I'd much rather buy something handmade, since it feels more personal and you know someone has put real care into it.

Do you think you would enjoy working in a factory? Why / why not?

Probably not on a production line, because I think the repetitive tasks would drive me crazy. That said, I'd be quite interested in a technical role, like programming robots or overseeing quality control, since it would involve solving problems rather than doing the same thing all day.

  2. 2. Coastal towns were so ________ on fishing that the collapse of the industry left them with almost nothing. (depend)
  3. 3. The ________ of the wetland took more than ten years and involved hundreds of local volunteers. (restore)

THE SEA THAT DISAPPEARED

1 Half a century ago, the Aral Sea, which lies on the border between Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan, was the fourth-largest lake on Earth, covering more than 60,000 square kilometres. Fishing fleets worked its waters, and towns along its shores depended on it for food, jobs and even a milder local climate. Today, most of that water has gone, and the Aral has become one of the most frequently quoted examples of what water scarcity caused by human activity can look like. Its story is a warning that reaches far beyond Central Asia.

2 The decline did not stem from drought or natural change. From the 1960s onwards, planners decided that the region's two great rivers, the Amu Darya and the Syr Darya, should feed a vast expansion of irrigation for cotton and other thirsty crops. Thousands of kilometres of canals were dug, and so much water was diverted that only a small fraction of the rivers' flow ever reached the sea. Many of the canals were unlined, so huge volumes were lost to evaporation and seepage long before they arrived at the fields.

3 As the shoreline retreated, in places by more than a hundred kilometres, the fishing industry collapsed. Ports such as Moynaq in Karakalpakstan found themselves stranded in the desert, their rusting ships now a grim attraction for visitors. Tens of thousands of people who had depended on the sea lost their livelihoods, and many younger residents left to look for work elsewhere. For those who stayed, the economic damage was accompanied by a painful sense that a whole way of life had disappeared within a single generation.

4 The environmental effects were equally severe. As the volume of water fell, its salinity rose sharply, eventually becoming too high for most native fish species to survive. The exposed seabed, now often called the Aralkum Desert, is covered in salt and the residue of agricultural chemicals that once washed into the sea. Strong winds lift this material into dust storms that can travel hundreds of kilometres, damaging crops and, according to many health studies, contributing to respiratory illness among local people.

5 Not everything has been lost, however. In 2005, Kazakhstan completed the Kok-Aral Dam, which separated the smaller northern part of the sea from the larger southern basin. Water levels in the North Aral rose noticeably within a few years, salinity fell, and commercially valuable fish returned, allowing a modest fishing industry to restart. The project showed that even after catastrophic damage, carefully targeted engineering can bring about real improvement, although the southern part of the sea has continued to shrink.

6 On the Uzbek side, attention has turned to the dried seabed itself. Large-scale planting of saxaul, a hardy desert shrub with deep roots, aims to hold the salty soil in place and mitigate the dust storms that blow across the region. International organisations have supported these efforts alongside projects to improve health care, drinking water and local employment. Few experts expect the southern sea to return, but stabilising the land around it is widely seen as an achievable goal.

7 The wider lesson concerns how Central Asia shares its water. The Amu Darya and Syr Darya are transboundary rivers, flowing through several countries whose needs do not always match: upstream states value water for hydropower in winter, while downstream farmers need it most in summer. Population growth and the gradual melting of mountain glaciers add further pressure. Efficient drip irrigation, repaired canals and closer regional cooperation are widely seen as the most realistic way to prevent the mistakes of the past from being repeated.

BRINGING NATURE BACK

1. For most of the twentieth century, conservation meant protecting what was left: drawing a line around a forest or wetland and keeping people out. Rewilding takes a more ambitious approach. Instead of simply preserving fragments of wild land, it aims to restore whole ecosystems that have been degraded by farming, logging or development, and then allow natural processes to take over. The idea has spread rapidly over the past three decades, from national parks in North America to former farmland in Europe, and it now attracts support from scientists, landowners and governments alike.

2. The best-known example comes from Yellowstone National Park in the United States, where grey wolves had been hunted to local extinction by the 1920s. Their reintroduction in 1995 is often credited with triggering a cascade of ecological change. With predators back, elk began to avoid certain valleys and riverbanks, allowing willow and aspen to recover in places. Researchers still debate how large these effects have really been, since drought, hunting and other factors also played a part, but the case transformed public thinking about how predators shape the landscapes around them.

3. In Britain, attention has focused on a smaller animal: the beaver, which disappeared from the country several centuries ago. Beavers are widely regarded as a keystone species, because the dams they build create ponds and wetlands that many other creatures depend on. Trial releases have shown that these dams can slow the flow of water after heavy rain, reducing flood peaks downstream, while also trapping sediment and pollutants. In 2022, wild beavers in England were given legal protection, a clear sign of how far official attitudes have shifted.

4. Rewilding is not only about reintroducing famous animals. At the Knepp Estate in southern England, the owners abandoned intensive farming around the turn of the century after years of financial losses. Rather than planting trees or managing habitats closely, they kept human intervention to a minimum, letting free-roaming cattle, pigs and deer graze the land as wild herbivores once would have done. Within two decades, the former fields had turned into a patchwork of scrub, grassland and young woodland, and rare birds such as nightingales and turtle doves had returned in significant numbers.

5. The approach has its critics, however. Sceptics point out that rewilding can conflict with food production at a time when the global population is still growing, and some farmers worry that returning predators will attack their livestock. In the Netherlands, a project at Oostvaardersplassen attracted strong public criticism when large numbers of grazing animals died during a harsh winter, raising difficult questions about how 'wild' a managed landscape should really be. Supporters respond that rewilding works best when local communities are involved from the start and share in its benefits.

6. Despite these debates, the case for restoring damaged land is growing stronger. Healthy ecosystems store carbon, filter water and protect soils, and areas rich in biodiversity tend to be more resilient when they face drought, disease or extreme weather. In a world where climate change is putting pressure on every landscape, rewilding offers something rare in environmental news: evidence that damage can, at least partly, be undone. It will never replace the need to cut emissions, but it suggests that nature, given enough space and time, is often capable of healing itself.

GRAMMAR FOR WRITING
GRAMMARNominalisation and cause–effect structures

Academic writers often turn verbs and adjectives into nouns (nominalisation), which allows them to pack more information into a sentence and to focus on processes rather than on people. This noun-based style combines naturally with formal cause–effect expressions such as result in, stem from, owing to and as a consequence of.

The rules below explain how to form noun phrases from verbs and adjectives, and which cause–effect structures are followed by a noun, a clause or a new sentence.

1. Nominalisation: change a verb or adjective into a noun (shrink → shrinkage, scarce → scarcity, reintroduce → reintroduction) and use it as the subject or object of the sentence.

The sea shrank rapidly, which shocked scientists. → The rapid shrinkage of the sea shocked scientists.

2. Use result in / lead to / give rise to + noun when the CAUSE comes first and the EFFECT follows the verb.

Poor maintenance of the canals resulted in huge water losses.

3. Use stem from / result from / arise from + noun when the EFFECT comes first and the CAUSE follows the verb. Do not confuse result in (→ effect) with result from (← cause).

Many of the region's health problems stem from salt and dust storms.

4. Owing to / due to / because of are followed by a noun phrase, not a full clause. Before a clause, use owing to the fact that.

Owing to the rise in salinity, most native fish disappeared. / Owing to the fact that salinity rose, most native fish disappeared.

5. As a consequence of / as a result of + noun introduce a cause within the sentence; As a consequence, / Consequently, (+ comma) begin a new sentence that describes an effect.

As a consequence of the dam's construction, water levels rose. Fish returned to the lake. Consequently, the fishing industry restarted.

6. Nominalisation makes these structures possible: a clause with a verb becomes a noun phrase that can follow result in, owing to, etc.

Because wolves were reintroduced, the elk changed their behaviour. → The reintroduction of wolves led to a change in elk behaviour.

ACADEMIC WRITINGWriting about causes and effects — showing how events are connected
ACADEMIC WRITING SKILLWriting about causes and effects

Cause-and-effect writing explains why something happens and what follows from it. A strong paragraph makes the direction of each relationship clear, avoids overstating certainty (may contribute to rather than simply causes), and often shows a chain in which one effect becomes the cause of the next.

CAUSE → EFFECT: Large-scale irrigation reduced the flow of both rivers, which in turn led to the shrinking of the sea.

EFFECT ← CAUSE: The collapse of the fishing industry stemmed largely from the sharp rise in salinity.

  5. 5  Plastic waste dumped in rivers eventually results in the pollution of the sea.
  6. 6  Owing to a long period of drought, several villages have had to rely on deliveries of drinking water.

Phrases & Idioms Wordlist

Carbon footprint: The total amount of greenhouse gases produced by a person, organisation or activity.

The tip of the iceberg: A small, visible part of a much larger problem that is mostly hidden.

A drop in the ocean: An amount so small compared with what is needed that it makes almost no difference.

Nip (something) in the bud: To stop a problem at an early stage, before it can grow or develop.

Can't see the wood for the trees: To be so focused on small details that you fail to understand the overall situation.

Weather the storm: To survive a difficult period without serious damage.

Muddy the waters: To make a situation more confusing or harder to understand.

Dead in the water: Having failed, or having no chance of succeeding or making progress.

Out of the woods: Free from danger or difficulty (often used in the negative: not out of the woods yet).

Reap what you sow: To experience the consequences, usually bad, of your own earlier actions.

Turn over a new leaf: To change your behaviour and start acting in a better, more responsible way.

Take a leaf out of someone's book: To copy something good that another person does.

The point of no return: The stage at which it is no longer possible to stop or reverse a process.

Bone dry: Completely dry, with no moisture at all.

Make hay while the sun shines: To take advantage of a good situation while it lasts.

WRITING PART 2

USEFUL LANGUAGE — Opinion essay

FunctionUseful phrases
Introducing the topicIn recent years, there has been growing concern about… / It is often argued that…
Stating your positionI firmly believe that… / In my view, … / I would argue that…
Explaining causes and effectsThis stems largely from… / As a consequence, … / This, in turn, results in…
Giving examplesA clear example of this is… / This can be seen in the case of…
Conceding the other sideAdmittedly, … / While it is true that…, … / Some would counter that…
ConcludingIn conclusion, … / On balance, I believe that… / To sum up, …

THE TASK

You are writing an essay for an academic audience. Write 180–200 words.

Some people believe that environmental problems such as water shortages are too large for individuals to solve, and that only governments and international organisations can make a real difference. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

PARAGRAPH PLAN

Introductionparaphrase the question + state your position (e.g. partly agree)
Body paragraph 1why governments and organisations are essential — scale, laws, infrastructure + an example
Body paragraph 2why individuals still matter — everyday habits, combined impact, public pressure
Conclusionsummarise both sides and restate your opinion in different words

RULES for Part 2 (essay)

☐  Answer the exact question — say clearly how far you agree, and keep this position consistent throughout.

☐  Aim for 180–200 words in four clear paragraphs: introduction, two body paragraphs, conclusion.

☐  Begin each body paragraph with a topic sentence, then support it with a reason and a specific example.

☐  Use a formal, impersonal register: no contractions, no slang, and avoid addressing the reader directly.

☐  Show a range of grammar and vocabulary — nominalisation, cause–effect expressions and topic collocations.

☐  Paraphrase the question in your introduction rather than copying it word for word.

SAMPLE ANSWER

In recent years, there has been growing concern about environmental problems such as water shortages and the loss of natural habitats. Some people argue that these issues are simply too large for ordinary citizens to tackle and that responsibility lies entirely with governments. While I accept that state action is essential, I would argue that individuals also have a meaningful role to play.

Admittedly, the sheer scale of many environmental crises means that only governments can address their root causes. The shrinking of the Aral Sea, for instance, stemmed from national decisions to divert entire rivers for irrigation, and only large-scale investment, such as modernising canals or building dams, can reverse damage of this kind. Similarly, laws on pollution and water use carry a weight that no single person can match.

Nevertheless, individual choices are far from insignificant. When millions of households waste less water or reduce their consumption, the combined effect can be considerable. Moreover, citizens who raise awareness and vote for greener policies put pressure on their leaders, which in turn results in stronger government action.

In conclusion, although governments and international bodies must lead the response to major environmental problems, individuals are by no means powerless. Real progress depends on both working together.

SPEAKING PART 2
QUESTIONS

Describe a natural place you know that has changed over time.

You should say:

☐  where the place is and what it used to be like

☐  how it has changed

☐  what has caused these changes

…and say how you feel about these changes and whether anything should be done about them.

SAMPLE ANSWER

I'd like to talk about a river near my grandparents' village in the Fergana Valley, which holds a special place in my heart because I spent almost every summer there as a child. Back then, it was wide and fast-flowing, and in the evenings the whole village seemed to gather along its banks to swim, fish or simply escape the heat.

Over the past ten years or so, though, it has changed almost beyond recognition. In late summer the water level drops so low that you can practically walk across it, and the fish my grandfather used to catch have become quite rare. Some of the trees along the bank have also been cut down to make room for new houses.

As far as I understand, the changes stem mainly from a combination of factors: more water is taken upstream for farming, the population has grown, and summers seem to be getting hotter and drier. As a consequence, there's simply less water to go round.

To be honest, I find it quite sad, because the river used to be such a central part of village life. I do think something can be done, though — for example, repairing irrigation channels so less water is wasted, and planting trees along the banks again. It might only be a drop in the ocean, but if local people work together, I'm hopeful the river could recover at least partly.

USEFUL LANGUAGE
Introducing the topic:I'd like to talk about… / A place that has changed a lot over the years is…
Describing the place:Back then, it was… / What I remember most clearly is… / It used to be…
Describing change:It has changed beyond recognition… / Compared to when I was a child, it's now…
Explaining causes:This stems mainly from… / The main reason seems to be… / As a consequence, …
Expressing feelings:To be honest, I find it quite sad/worrying… / It really bothers me that…
Concluding / looking ahead:I do think something can be done… / Overall, I'm hopeful that…

  7. 7 A growing body of research links regular access to green space with improved mental well-being.
  8. 8 During rush hour, the city's congested roads can turn a ten-minute journey into an hour-long ordeal.

WHAT MAKES A PLACE LIVEABLE?

1 Ask people to describe a place they genuinely enjoy spending time in, and very few will mention a record-breaking skyscraper or a vast glass shopping mall. Far more often, they describe a shaded square, a lively street market or a quiet courtyard where neighbours stop to talk. Architects and planners call this quality 'liveability': the extent to which a building or public space supports the everyday lives of the people who use it. It is rarely a matter of size or spectacle. What makes a place liveable is usually the sum of many small, carefully considered details.

2 One of the most influential ideas in modern urban design is 'human scale' — the principle that buildings and streets should be measured against the human body rather than the motor car. Someone walking at five kilometres an hour notices doorways, windows, textures and trees; a driver at sixty notices almost nothing. Streets lined with buildings of three to six storeys, with shops and cafés at ground level, tend to feel intimate and safe, whereas a plaza surrounded by blank forty-storey towers can feel exposed and empty, however impressive it looks on an architect's model.

3 For much of the twentieth century, cities were redesigned around traffic. Wide roads were cut through old neighbourhoods, and streets became places to pass through rather than places to be. Today, many cities are reversing that trend. Turning congested shopping streets into pedestrian zones was once dismissed as bad for business, yet study after study has found that people on foot linger longer and, over time, spend more than drivers who park, shop and leave. Cleaner air and quieter streets, it turns out, are good for trade as well as for health.

4 Liveability also depends on what happens inside buildings. So-called green buildings aim to use as little energy as possible while keeping the people inside them comfortable. Many achieve this by borrowing ideas that traditional builders understood centuries ago: thick walls that store heat during the day, courtyards that draw cool air through rooms, and windows positioned for natural ventilation instead of relying entirely on air conditioning. Not only do such features cut energy bills, but they also create healthier indoor environments, since stale air and poor light are closely linked to tiredness and headaches.

5 Perhaps surprisingly, many architects now argue that the greenest building is the one that already exists. Constructing a new building releases enormous amounts of carbon, from producing cement and steel to transporting materials to the site. Choosing to retrofit an existing structure — adding insulation, solar panels, efficient heating and better windows — often achieves similar energy savings at a fraction of the environmental cost. As a result, demolition, once seen as the obvious first step in any redevelopment project, is increasingly treated as a last resort.

6 Liveability is equally a question of distance. Low-density urban sprawl, with housing estates miles away from shops and workplaces, forces residents to drive for almost every errand and leaves those without a car isolated. In response, planners in cities from Paris to Melbourne have promoted the idea of the 'fifteen-minute city', in which schools, clinics, parks and other everyday amenities are within a short walk or bike ride of home. The aim is not to stop people travelling further, but to make sure they no longer have to.

7 Finally, there is the question of nature. Research consistently shows that access to trees, parks and water improves physical health and mental well-being, lowers stress and even reduces summer temperatures in densely built areas. Yet the most liveable places are rarely designed by experts alone. It is often residents, through years of small adjustments — a bench added here, a vegetable garden there — who turn a well-planned space into a genuinely loved one. A building can win every award going and still fail if nobody wants to spend time there.

LANGUAGE DEVELOPMENT - Describing urban change

VOCABULARY SKILLVerb + noun collocations

When we write about how cities change, certain verbs combine naturally with a small group of nouns — for example preserve the character of an area, or tackle congestion. Learning these as fixed chunks, rather than word by word, helps you describe planning and architecture precisely and sound more natural in academic writing.

restorea building, a monument, a facade (to its original condition)
preserveheritage, the character, the atmosphere (of a place)
demolisha building, a tower block, a structure
revitalisea neighbourhood, a city centre, a run-down area
tacklecongestion, pollution, urban sprawl
enhancewell-being, quality of life, the appeal (of an area)

OLD WALLS, NEW CITIES

1. Walk through the old centre of almost any Central Asian city and you are walking through layers of history: mosques and madrasas, covered bazaars, bathhouses and caravanserais that once served merchants travelling the Silk Road. Cities such as Samarkand and Bukhara attract visitors from all over the world precisely because so much of this past is still standing. Yet these same cities are home to growing populations who need housing, roads, schools and jobs. How to balance the protection of the past with the demands of the present is one of the most difficult questions facing planners today.

2. Supporters of new construction point out that not every old building is worth saving. Many historic quarters contain dilapidated houses with crumbling walls, poor sanitation and no proper heating, and the families living in them often want modern homes rather than romantic surroundings. Repairing such buildings can cost far more than replacing them, and in some cases demolition is the only safe option. A city, they argue, is not a museum; it must be allowed to change if it is to remain a good place in which to live and work.

3. Conservationists respond that once a historic building is lost, it is lost for ever. They also warn against restoration that goes too far. When ancient structures are rebuilt with new materials and bright, perfectly uniform tiles, they may look impressive in photographs, but they lose much of their authenticity. Some developers keep only the historic facade of a building and replace everything behind it with offices or hotel rooms — a compromise that critics compare to keeping the cover of a book while throwing away all of its pages.

4. A further concern is what happens to the people who actually live in historic areas. Successful restoration often attracts tourists, boutique hotels and expensive restaurants, and with them comes gentrification: property prices rise, long-standing residents sell up or are priced out, and local workshops and corner shops are replaced by souvenir stalls. The result can be an old town that is beautifully preserved but strangely sterile, crowded with visitors during the day and almost empty of residents at night, its streets quiet once the tour groups have gone.

5. International bodies such as UNESCO try to manage these pressures by protecting not only individual monuments but also the 'buffer zones' around them. Within these zones, the height and style of new buildings are strictly controlled, so that modern development does not encroach on the historic skyline. Many experts believe the most effective approach is to concentrate large new projects — business districts, apartment towers, transport hubs — outside the historic core, where they can grow freely without overshadowing the monuments that give the city its identity.

6. In the end, preservation and development need not be opposites. Some of the most successful projects give old buildings new purposes: a caravanserai converted into a crafts centre, a former bathhouse reopened as a gallery, a merchant's house turned into a small guesthouse run by the family that owns it. When local communities are treated as the true custodians of their heritage, rather than as obstacles to tourism, historic centres can remain what they were always meant to be — living places, not open-air museums.

GRAMMAR FOR WRITING
GRAMMARCleft sentences & fronting for emphasis

Writers often rearrange a sentence to draw the reader's attention to its most important idea. Cleft sentences split one clause into two parts so that the key information is placed in focus, while fronting moves a word or phrase to the beginning of a sentence, sometimes with inversion of the subject and auxiliary.

The rules below show the most common ways to add emphasis in formal and academic writing.

1. What-clefts: What + clause + is/was + the focus. Use them to highlight an action, a thing or an idea.

What makes a square feel welcoming is the sense of enclosure created by low buildings.

2. It-clefts: It is/was + the focus + that/who + the rest of the clause. Use them to emphasise one particular person, thing, time or reason, often in contrast to another.

It was the residents, not the planners, who saved the old bathhouse from demolition.

3. All / The thing / The reason (why) / The place (where) can replace What to give a slightly different emphasis.

All the old quarter really needs is careful, regular maintenance.

4. Negative and limiting adverbials (Not only, Never, Rarely, Seldom, Little) can be fronted for emphasis. The subject and auxiliary are then inverted.

Not only do green roofs reduce energy bills, but they also help to prevent flooding.

5. Only + time expression (Only after / Only when / Only then) is followed by inversion in the main clause, not in the time clause.

Only when the facade was cleaned did its original colours become visible.

6. Fronted adjective or prepositional phrase + be/verb + subject is used in descriptive writing to emphasise a feature.

Particularly striking is the blue-tiled dome that rises above the market.

ACADEMIC WRITINGComparing and contrasting — showing similarities and differences
ACADEMIC WRITING SKILLComparing and contrasting

When you compare and contrast, you show how two places, ideas or approaches are similar or different. Use expressions such as similarly, likewise and in much the same way to show similarity, and whereas, while, by contrast and conversely to show difference. Note that whereas and while join two clauses in one sentence, while by contrast, conversely and similarly usually begin a new sentence and are followed by a comma.

COMPARING: Trees cool the streets beneath them. In much the same way, green roofs lower the temperature of the buildings they cover.

CONTRASTING: Whereas many new districts are designed around the car, historic centres were built for people on foot.

Join each pair of ideas into one or two sentences, using the expression in brackets to compare or contrast them.

  1. 1  Old city centres were built for walking. / Modern suburbs are designed around the car. (whereas)
  2. 2  Restoration preserves a building's history. / New construction allows modern standards of comfort and safety. (conversely)
  3. 3  Parks improve residents' mental health. / Tree-lined streets reduce stress. (in much the same way)
  4. 4  Glass towers are expensive to cool in summer. / Traditional mud-brick houses stay cool naturally. (by contrast)
  5. 5  Samarkand depends heavily on tourism to its historic monuments. / Bukhara relies on its heritage to attract visitors. (similarly)
  6. 6  Some planners favour high-rise housing to save land. / Others argue that low-rise districts are more liveable. (while)

INDIA

I. The world’s first university was established in India in 700 BC, where more than 10,500 students from around the world studied more than 60 different subjects. The training was conducted in Sanskrit. Nowadays, Sanskrit is considered to be the mother of all the European languages. Its elements can be traced in most of them.

II. The most frequently visited place in India is Delhi, the capital city of the country. It seems to be divided into two parts. New Delhi is a modern city with hi-tech architecture, tourist attractions and modern facilities. Old Delhi is several centuries old, with narrow streets, ancient churches and noisy bazaars. Lots of people live in slums without the most essential facilities like toilets and running water.

III. People all over the world know of India’s greatest river, the Ganges. The river looks extremely beautiful in the morning light. It is the subject of thousands of prayers. It has become a common ritual for pilgrims to gather by the holy river in the mornings. It is believed that bathing in the Ganges helps to cure all kinds of diseases and can improve your life in general.

IV. Indian climate differs from one part of the country to another. The air is cool and fresh in the mountains, but in the plains it is usually very hot and dry, so even a short trip can be very hard for an inexperienced traveller. That is why tourists are always glad to have a rest at one of the numerous stations in the hills. There they can enjoy a nice cup of real Indian tea, the most refreshing drink in such a climate.

V. India is not all history. It is also famous for its Bollywood industry, which produces different films. Indian films have always had their own style; they are rich in music and dancing. Though the industry is still developing, many Indian film stars have received Oscar prizes and are known throughout the world. The home of Bollywood is Mumbai, also known as a busy port and the country’s commercial centre.

VI. There is an unusual treasure hidden in the Indian mountains. These are striking ancient temples cut in the rocks. For example, the Buddhist cave temples at Ajanta were built at least 2,000 years ago. Inside the caves on the walls, tourists can see animal images and pictures of people’s lives. Some researchers believe that the interpretation of the images can help us to learn a lot about people’s lives in ancient times.

Phrases & Idioms Wordlist

Lay the foundations (for something): To create the basic conditions from which something can develop and succeed.

Concrete jungle: A city area full of large, unattractive buildings, with little greenery or open space.

Bricks and mortar: Buildings, especially seen as property or a physical shop rather than an online business.

Hit the roof: To become suddenly very angry.

Go through the roof: (of prices or numbers) To rise very quickly to a very high level.

Under one roof: All together in the same building or organisation.

Built to last: Made so strongly or well that it will survive for a long time.

Hit a brick wall: To reach a point where you cannot make any further progress.

The writing is on the wall: There are clear signs that something is going to fail or come to an end.

Rome wasn't built in a day: Important or ambitious projects take a long time to complete.

A stone's throw (from): A very short distance away; very close to.

Set in stone: Fixed and impossible to change.

The cornerstone (of something): The most important part, on which everything else is based.

Off the beaten track: Far away from the places that most people visit; quiet and little-known.

Paint the town red: To go out in the city and celebrate in a lively, noisy way.

SAMPLE ANSWER

Dear Chairperson,

Thank you for informing members about the council's plans to redevelop the old market square. I must admit that I was deeply disappointed to learn that several of the historic trading houses may be demolished, as they give our neighbourhood much of its character.

While I understand that parking is a genuine problem in the area, I do not believe that a multi-storey car park is the right solution. What the square really needs is careful restoration. I would suggest that the trading houses be repaired and converted into small shops, cafés and workshops for local craftspeople. Not only would this preserve our heritage, but it would also attract visitors and support local businesses.

Furthermore, it might be worth considering a car park on the edge of the district, connected to the square by a pleasant pedestrian street with trees and benches.

I would be grateful if you could pass these suggestions on to the council. I look forward to hearing about the outcome.

Yours faithfully,

D. Rakhimova

SPEAKING PART 3
STATEMENT

Historic buildings should be preserved at all costs, even if this slows down a city's development.

Discuss both sides of the statement and give your own opinion. Use the points below to help you.

FORAGAINST
Once a historic building is destroyed, it can never be replaced.Many old buildings are unsafe, unhealthy or too expensive to repair.
Heritage sites attract tourists and bring income to local people.Growing populations urgently need modern housing, roads and services.
Old buildings give a city its identity and a sense of continuity.Over-protection can turn a living city into a sterile museum.
SAMPLE ANSWER

I'd like to begin by saying that I partly agree with this statement. On the one hand, historic buildings are irreplaceable. What makes cities like Samarkand and Bukhara so special is that their past is still visible in their streets, and once a madrasa or a caravanserai has been knocked down, no amount of money can bring it back. On top of that, heritage is a major source of income, because tourists travel thousands of kilometres to see these places.

On the other hand, I think the phrase 'at all costs' goes too far. Not every old building is worth saving — some are genuinely dilapidated and unsafe, and the families living in them deserve proper heating, clean water and modern facilities. Whereas a monument of world importance should obviously be protected, an ordinary run-down block from the last century is a very different case. Besides, a city that is never allowed to change risks becoming sterile — a beautiful museum where nobody actually lives.

On balance, I believe the best solution is a compromise. It is the most important monuments that should be protected strictly, while large new projects are built outside the historic core. Old buildings can also be given new purposes, such as galleries or guesthouses, so that they stay alive. All things considered, development and preservation can go hand in hand if they are planned carefully.

USEFUL LANGUAGE
Giving your overall view:I partly/strongly agree that... / I'm not entirely convinced that...
Presenting one side:On the one hand, ... / What makes ... so special is... / One strong argument in favour is...
Presenting the other side:On the other hand, ... / Having said that, ... / It could be argued that...
Comparing and contrasting:Whereas..., ... / By contrast, ... / In much the same way, ...
Adding a point:On top of that, ... / Besides, ... / Not only..., but also...
Concluding:On balance, ... / All things considered, ... / The best solution, in my view, is...

  3. 3. Families who ________ their lofts and walls properly can cut their heating bills by up to a third. (insulate)
  4. 4. Sharp ________ in the price of gas made it almost impossible for small businesses to plan ahead. (fluctuations)
  5. 5. In the early years, rooftop solar panels were heavily ________ by the state to encourage people to buy them. (subsidised)

THE AGE OF SUN AND WIND

1 For most of the twentieth century, generating electricity meant burning something — coal, oil or gas — and very few people imagined that sunlight and moving air could ever seriously compete. Yet over the past fifteen years, the world has entered a genuine energy transition, and it has happened far faster than even the most optimistic forecasts predicted. In several countries, solar and wind now provide more power than coal on a typical sunny or breezy day, and new records are broken every year, often with surprisingly little public attention.

2 The single biggest reason is cost. The price of solar panels has fallen by roughly ninety per cent since 2010, while wind turbines have become larger, more efficient and far cheaper to run. For years, renewable projects depended on generous government subsidies to attract investors, and critics argued that they would never survive without them. Today, in many markets, a new solar farm is the cheapest way to produce electricity, which means that clean energy has become commercially viable on its own terms rather than simply a political choice.

3 Nowhere is the potential clearer than in sunny, wide-open regions. Countries across Central Asia, the Middle East and North Africa receive intense sunshine for most of the year and have large areas of flat, sparsely populated land. Governments there have begun to harness this natural advantage with vast solar parks covering thousands of hectares, often built in partnership with foreign investors. Some projects are designed not only to supply domestic cities but, in time, to export electricity to neighbouring states, turning land once dismissed as empty into a valuable economic asset.

4 However, sun and wind share a fundamental weakness: they are intermittent. Panels produce nothing at night, output drops on cloudy days, and even the windiest coastline experiences calm spells that can last for a week. Demand for electricity, by contrast, does not stop when the weather changes; hospitals, factories and homes need a reliable supply around the clock. Grid operators must therefore keep backup power available, and matching an unpredictable supply with constant demand is arguably the central problem of the renewable age.

5 Wind power, meanwhile, is moving out to sea. Offshore turbines benefit from stronger and steadier winds than those on land, and because they are far from homes, they can be built on an enormous scale. A single modern turbine can now stand taller than many skyscrapers, with blades longer than a football pitch, and its generating capacity is many times that of the machines installed twenty years ago. A handful of these giants can power an entire town, although building them in deep, stormy waters remains expensive and technically demanding.

6 Producing clean electricity is only half the task; it also has to reach the people who use it. The best solar and wind sites are frequently hundreds of kilometres from major cities, so new high-voltage power lines must be deployed across mountains, farmland and national borders. Such projects can take a decade to approve, and they sometimes face fierce resistance from residents who object to their visual impact, or from farmers who are reluctant to give up productive land for endless rows of panels.

7 Despite these obstacles, many governments have now committed to phase out coal entirely within the next two decades, and some have set dates to end the sale of new petrol and diesel cars. The shift brings real social challenges, particularly for communities whose jobs have depended on mining for generations. Yet it is also creating entirely new industries, from panel installation to turbine maintenance. The question is no longer whether the world will move to renewable energy, but how quickly — and how fairly — that move can be managed.
