KEEPING THE LIGHTS ON

1. If the great challenge of renewable energy is that the sun does not always shine, the obvious solution is to save electricity when there is too much and release it when there is too little. On a bright spring afternoon, solar farms can produce such a large surplus that wholesale prices briefly fall below zero and some users are effectively paid to consume power. A few hours later, as people return home, cook dinner and switch on their televisions, the same grid may be struggling to cope. Storage is the bridge between those two moments.

2. The most familiar form of storage is the lithium-ion battery, the same technology found in phones and electric cars. Over the past decade, huge battery installations, some the size of several football pitches, have been connected to grids around the world. They can respond to a sudden drop in supply within a fraction of a second, far faster than any conventional power station. Their main limitation is duration: most can deliver power for only a few hours, which is enough to cover the evening peak but not a windless week in winter.

3. For longer periods, engineers are turning to older and more unusual ideas. Pumped hydro, which uses spare electricity to pump water uphill into a reservoir and then releases it through turbines when needed, still provides the vast majority of the world's stored energy. Other projects store heat in tanks of molten salt, compress air in underground caverns or convert excess power into hydrogen. None of these methods is perfect, and costs vary considerably, but together they could make a grid built on sun and wind as reliable as the fossil-fuel systems it replaces.

4. Storage is only one part of the answer; the other is managing demand more intelligently. A so-called smart grid uses digital meters and automated systems to track how much electricity is being used, minute by minute. Because wholesale prices can fluctuate dramatically during the day, smart meters allow suppliers to charge less when power is plentiful and more when it is scarce. Customers then have a financial incentive to run washing machines, dishwashers or car chargers overnight or at midday, spreading demand more evenly and reducing the need for expensive backup plants.

5. Perhaps the cheapest unit of energy, however, is the one that is never used. In many countries, homes account for around a quarter of total energy consumption, much of it lost through badly sealed windows, thin walls and uninsulated roofs. Improving insulation can cut heating bills significantly, and governments increasingly offer grants to help owners retrofit older buildings with double glazing, heat pumps or rooftop panels. Small habits matter too: lowering the thermostat by a single degree, or switching devices off rather than leaving them on standby, makes a noticeable difference over a year.

6. None of these changes is dramatic on its own, and that is precisely their strength. The energy system of the future is likely to combine large-scale storage, flexible smart grids and millions of efficient homes, each playing a modest role. Policies that curb waste while rewarding households for using power at the right time may prove just as important as building new wind farms. In other words, keeping the lights on in a renewable world depends not only on engineers and governments, but also on the everyday choices made in ordinary kitchens and living rooms.

GRAMMAR FOR WRITING
GRAMMARFuture forms for predictions and degrees of certainty

When writers make predictions, they rarely present every future event as equally certain. Academic and journalistic texts use a range of future forms to show how confident the writer is, whether something has already been planned, and whether an action will be in progress or completed at a particular point in the future.

The rules below show how to choose the future form that matches your degree of certainty and the timing of the event.

1. Use will / won't + infinitive for general predictions based on opinion or knowledge. Add probably, almost certainly or definitely to show how sure you are (after will, before won't).

Solar power will almost certainly become cheaper, but it probably won't replace gas completely in the next decade.

2. Use be likely / unlikely to + infinitive (or It is likely that …) to express probability in a more cautious, academic way.

Electricity demand is likely to double by 2050, and it is unlikely that coal will meet this demand.

3. Use be bound to / be certain to + infinitive when you are very confident that something will happen, often because it is logical or inevitable.

As battery prices fall, more households are bound to install storage at home.

4. Use be set to + infinitive for something that is planned, arranged or strongly expected to happen soon — very common in news reports.

The country's largest solar park is set to open next spring.

5. Use the future continuous (will be + -ing) for an action that will be in progress at a particular time in the future.

By the end of the decade, millions of cars will be charging from the grid every night.

6. Use the future perfect (will have + past participle) for an action that will be completed before a certain point in the future, often with by or by the time.

By 2040, most European countries will have closed their last coal-fired power station.

ACADEMIC WRITINGPresenting advantages and disadvantages — writing a balanced argument
ACADEMIC WRITING SKILLBalanced argument and signposting

In a balanced argument, the writer presents both the advantages and the disadvantages of an issue fairly before reaching a conclusion. Signposting phrases such as One major benefit is …, On the other hand, … and A further drawback is … guide the reader clearly from one side of the argument to the other.

ADVANTAGE: One clear benefit of rooftop solar panels is that, once installed, they produce electricity at almost no cost.

DISADVANTAGE: On the other hand, a significant drawback is that their output falls sharply at night and on cloudy days.

PIRATES

There have always been people who robbed ships in the open sea. We know them as pirates or corsairs. Many of them were sailors who lost their jobs, others were just young men and women looking for adventure. Thousands of pirates were active from 1650–1720. These years are sometimes known as the 'Golden Age' of piracy. Probably the most famous pirates of this period are Blackbeard, Henry Morgan, William 'Captain' Kidd, and the Barbarossa brothers.

The "Jolly Roger" is the well-known pirate flag. There are a number of theories about its origin. It is thought that the first pirates used a red flag, which was common in sea attacks. A red flag told other ships that there would be no pity and no prisoners would be taken. This red flag was called Joli Rouge (pretty red) in French. Most probably, English people pronounced it in their own way "Jolly Roger". Another theory says that "old Roger" was another name for the devil.

Another popular image from the pirate world is a parrot, sitting on the captain's shoulder. Well, there's no historical proof of that. No doubt, pirates often travelled to faraway exotic lands and brought unusual animals as souvenirs with them. Parrots were particularly popular because they were colourful, could be taught to speak, and were easier to care for than, say, monkeys. However, you can't imagine a pirate fighting with a bird on the shoulder. This image possibly began with the book "Treasure Island". In the book, the ever famous Long John Silver carried a parrot as a pet.

Before joining a ship each pirate signed an agreement called "Articles". This explained the rights and laws on board the ship, how much a person was paid, what to do in case of emergency, etc. For example, playing cards for money was not allowed. For breaking the rules a pirate would be shot or left on a desert island with a bottle of water and a gun.

A pirate ship was organized democratically. After a successful attack they divided the treasures equally, only the captain and the cook got more. They sometimes decided together which ship to attack or where to sail next. Most pirates were paid four times more than they had when they were sailors. But on land they were criminals and lots of money was offered to those who caught them.

However, for some time the English government supported pirates. There were lots of pirates in the sixteenth century when England was at war with Spain and the Dutch Republic. Queen Elizabeth I ordered them to rob Spanish ships and bring gold, silver and jewels to the country. Sir Francis Drake was one of the most famous pirates. He brought lots of treasures to England and also was the first Englishman to sail all the way around the world. Because of this, he was made a knight by Queen Elizabeth I.

Phrases & Idioms Wordlist

Run out of steam: To lose energy or enthusiasm and be unable to continue with the same effort.

Recharge your batteries: To rest and relax so that you have energy again.

Full of beans: Very lively, cheerful and full of energy.

Burn the candle at both ends: To work or stay active from early morning until late at night, leaving yourself exhausted.

Burn out: To become completely exhausted, physically or mentally, after working too hard for too long.

Get a second wind: To suddenly find new energy to continue after feeling tired.

Firing on all cylinders: Working or performing at full power and as well as possible.

Power through (something): To continue doing something difficult with determination until it is finished.

Running on empty: Continuing to work or function even though you have no energy or resources left.

Pull the plug on (something): To stop a project or activity suddenly, usually by stopping its funding.

Blow a fuse: To suddenly become very angry and lose your temper.

On the same wavelength: Having similar ideas and understanding each other well.

A live wire: A very lively, energetic and enthusiastic person.

Switch off: To stop paying attention or stop thinking about something, especially in order to relax.

Spark off (something): To cause something to start, especially a reaction, argument or series of events.

WRITING PART 2

USEFUL LANGUAGE — Advantages and disadvantages essay

FunctionUseful phrases
Introducing the topicIn recent years, … / It is widely accepted that … / A growing number of countries have …
Presenting advantagesOne major benefit of … is that … / The most obvious advantage is … / A further point in its favour is …
Presenting disadvantagesOn the other hand, … / However, a significant drawback is … / Critics point out that …
Adding pointsFurthermore, … / In addition, … / What is more, …
Making predictions… is likely to … / … is bound to … / By 2040, … will have …
Concluding / giving your viewOn balance, I believe … / Overall, the benefits clearly outweigh the drawbacks … / To sum up, …

THE TASK

You are writing an essay for an academic audience. Write 180–200 words.

Many governments are now spending large amounts of money on solar and wind farms instead of traditional power stations. What are the advantages and disadvantages of this trend? Give your own opinion.

PARAGRAPH PLAN

Introductionparaphrase the question + say that the trend has both benefits and drawbacks
Body paragraph 1advantages: environment, falling costs, energy independence + examples
Body paragraph 2disadvantages: intermittent supply, cost of storage and power lines, land use
Conclusionweigh up both sides + give your overall opinion clearly

RULES for Part 2 (essay)

☐  Answer ALL parts of the question — advantages, disadvantages AND your own opinion.

☐  Write 180–200 words in four clear paragraphs: introduction, two body paragraphs and a conclusion.

☐  Use a formal, academic register: no contractions, no slang and no direct questions to the reader.

☐  Begin each body paragraph with a clear topic sentence and use signposting phrases to move between ideas.

☐  Support each main point with a reason or an example, and use cautious future forms (is likely to, is set to) for predictions.

☐  Make your conclusion consistent with your argument — do not introduce new ideas at the end.

SAMPLE ANSWER

In recent years, a growing number of governments have chosen to invest in solar and wind farms rather than power stations that burn coal or gas. While this shift offers clear benefits, it also raises a number of practical concerns.

The most obvious advantage is environmental. Renewable sources produce virtually no greenhouse gases once they are operating, so they are bound to play a central role in tackling climate change. Furthermore, the cost of solar panels and turbines has fallen dramatically, which means that clean electricity is now often cheaper than power from fossil fuels. Sunny countries in particular are likely to benefit, as they can generate energy locally instead of importing expensive fuel.

On the other hand, there are significant drawbacks. Sun and wind are intermittent, so countries must also invest in batteries and new power lines, which adds considerably to the overall cost. In addition, large projects can occupy huge areas of land and sometimes face strong opposition from local residents.

On balance, I believe the advantages clearly outweigh the disadvantages. Although the transition will not be easy, governments that invest wisely in storage as well as generation will have built a cleaner and more secure energy system within a generation.

SPEAKING PART 2
QUESTIONS

Describe a time when you or your family tried to save energy at home.

You should say:

☐  when and why you decided to save energy

☐  what changes you made

☐  how easy or difficult it was to keep to these changes

…and say whether you think individuals can really make a difference to the amount of energy a country uses.

SAMPLE ANSWER

I'd like to talk about a winter about two years ago, when my family made a real effort to cut our energy bills. The trigger was a particularly cold month when our electricity and gas bill was almost double what we had expected, and my father announced, quite dramatically, that things had to change.

The first thing we did was sort out the insulation — we sealed the gaps around our old windows and put thick curtains up in the living room. We also got into the habit of switching devices off at the wall instead of leaving them on standby, and we replaced every old bulb with LED lights. My younger brother was put in charge of checking that lights were off in empty rooms, and to be honest, he took the job far more seriously than any of us expected.

Some changes were easy, but others were harder to stick to. Turning the heating down by a couple of degrees, for example, led to a few arguments, especially in the mornings! Still, after a couple of months the bills had dropped noticeably, which kept everyone motivated.

As for whether individuals can make a difference, I'd say on their own, probably not much, but millions of households doing the same things certainly can. At the end of the day, I think government policy and personal habits have to work together.

USEFUL LANGUAGE
Introducing the topic:I'd like to talk about a time when… / One experience that comes to mind is…
Explaining the reason:The main reason was… / What really prompted us to change was…
Describing changes:The first thing we did was… / We also got into the habit of…
Talking about difficulty:Some changes were easy, but… / It was quite hard to stick to…
Describing results:After a while, we noticed that… / The bills dropped noticeably…
Giving a wider opinion:On their own, individuals… / At the end of the day, I think…

  2. 2. Video calls have made it far more ________ for people in rural areas to get medical advice. (convenience)
  3. 3. The ________ of the new scanning software was tested on more than 10,000 images. (accurate)

THE RACE AGAINST RESISTANT BACTERIA

1 When penicillin entered hospitals in the 1940s, infections that had routinely killed patients suddenly became treatable within days. For several decades afterwards, it seemed that bacterial disease had been more or less defeated. Today, however, that confidence looks badly misplaced. Strains of bacteria that no longer respond to common antibiotics have emerged on every continent, and infections once considered minor — a scratch that turns septic, a urinary infection, a case of pneumonia — are becoming harder, and in some cases impossible, to treat.

2 The process behind this is, in principle, simple natural selection. Every time an antibiotic is used, the bacteria most susceptible to it die first, while any that happen to carry a protective mutation survive and multiply. Because bacteria reproduce so quickly, a resistant population can build up in a matter of weeks. Worse still, many bacteria can pass resistance genes directly to one another, so a defence that appears in one species may eventually spread to others that have never been exposed to the drug at all.

3 Human behaviour has accelerated this process considerably. In many countries, doctors under pressure from anxious patients prescribe antibiotics for colds and flu, even though these are viral illnesses that antibiotics cannot touch. Patients, in turn, often stop taking their tablets as soon as they feel better, leaving the toughest bacteria alive. Meanwhile, vast quantities of antibiotics are given to healthy farm animals simply to speed up their growth, creating ideal conditions for resistance to develop far away from any hospital ward.

4 The obvious answer would be to invent new drugs, yet this has proved remarkably difficult. Most antibiotics in use today belong to families discovered more than half a century ago. Researchers screening thousands of natural and synthetic compounds frequently find that promising candidates are either too toxic for humans or simply variations on drugs that bacteria have already learnt to resist. As one microbiologist put it, the easy discoveries were made long ago; what remains is slow, expensive and often disappointing work.

5 Even when a candidate looks viable, the road to the pharmacy is long. A new medicine must pass through laboratory testing, followed by several phases of clinical trials involving progressively larger groups of volunteers. Each stage is designed to answer a specific question — whether the drug is safe, what dose works, and whether it performs better than existing treatments — and the whole process typically takes ten years or more. This rigorous approach protects patients, but it also means that only a small fraction of the compounds that enter testing ever reach the market.

6 Here lies the central economic problem. A company that spends a decade developing a cancer drug or a medicine for a long-term condition can expect patients to buy it for years. A new antibiotic, by contrast, is likely to be held in reserve by doctors and used only as a last resort, precisely to slow the development of resistance. Low sales mean that pharmaceutical firms have little financial incentive to invest, and several large companies have withdrawn from antibiotic research altogether.

7 Governments and health organisations are now experimenting with alternative models, such as paying companies a fixed annual fee for access to a new antibiotic regardless of how often it is used. Scientists, meanwhile, are exploring options ranging from viruses that attack specific bacteria to artificial intelligence that can scan millions of molecules in days. None of these is a quick fix, but experts broadly agree on one point: unless prescribing habits change alongside the science, any new drug will eventually meet the same fate as the old ones.

THE DOCTOR WILL SEE YOU NOW — ON SCREEN

1. For most of medical history, seeing a doctor meant being in the same room. That assumption changed almost overnight during the COVID-19 pandemic, when clinics around the world switched to video and telephone consultations to keep patients and staff apart. Many expected the change to be temporary. Instead, remote care has become a permanent feature of many health systems, and it is now being joined by a second, potentially more disruptive technology: artificial intelligence that can help identify disease from scans, photographs and test results.

2. The benefits of telemedicine are easy to see, particularly for people who live far from a hospital or find travelling difficult. A farmer in a remote village can show a rash to a specialist hundreds of kilometres away; a parent can get advice about a feverish child without spending half a day in a crowded waiting room. For routine follow-up appointments and repeat prescriptions, supporters argue, the convenience and savings clearly outweigh the drawbacks of not meeting face to face.

3. AI diagnostic tools promise something different: speed and consistency. Systems trained on millions of medical images can now spot signs of certain eye diseases, skin cancers and lung conditions, in some studies matching the performance of experienced specialists. Unlike humans, they do not get tired or distracted at the end of a long shift. In countries with too few radiologists, hospitals have deployed such software to sort scans so that the most urgent cases are seen first, cutting potentially dangerous delays.

4. Yet these tools have come under increasing scrutiny. An algorithm is only as good as the data it learns from, and if that data comes mainly from one population, the system may perform poorly for others. Researchers have found evidence of bias in some programs designed to detect skin conditions, which were far less accurate on darker skin because few such images had been included in their training. Errors of this kind could deepen existing inequalities in health care rather than reduce them.

5. There are also difficult questions of responsibility. If an AI system misses a tumour, who should be held accountable — the doctor who relied on it, the hospital that bought it, or the company that built it? Current regulations were largely written for human professionals and conventional medical devices, and lawmakers in many countries are still debating how to adapt them. Patients, too, have concerns about privacy, since both video calls and AI systems depend on large amounts of sensitive personal data being stored and shared.

6. Most doctors see the future as a partnership rather than a replacement. Software may be better at detecting patterns in images, but a clinician's intuition, built over years of examining patients, can pick up on details that never appear in a scan — a hesitation in someone's voice, or a symptom the patient forgot to mention. And for many people, especially those facing a serious diagnosis, the reassurance of a calm conversation with another human being remains an essential part of being cared for.

GRAMMAR FOR WRITING
GRAMMARReporting verbs & reported speech in academic writing

Academic writers constantly report what other researchers have said, found or argued. The reporting verb you choose shows not only what a source says but also how strong the evidence is and how far you agree with it. Impersonal structures such as it has been found that allow you to report findings without naming a specific person.

The rules below show the main groups of reporting verbs, the patterns that follow them, and how the choice of verb changes the meaning of a sentence.

1. Neutral verbs — state, report, note, explain, observe + that — simply present what a source says without judging it.

The authors note that resistance rates have risen sharply over the last decade.

2. Tentative verbs — suggest, indicate, propose, imply — show that the evidence points towards something but is not conclusive.

The data suggest that shorter courses of antibiotics may be just as effective.

3. Strong verbs — argue, claim, maintain, insist — present a position the source is defending. Claim often signals that the writer has doubts about it.

The manufacturer claims that its app can detect skin cancer as accurately as a specialist.

4. Acknowledge, admit, concede show that a source accepts a point, often one that weakens its own argument.

Supporters of telemedicine acknowledge that video calls are unsuitable for some examinations.

5. Some verbs take different patterns: warn (sb) against + -ing, urge sb to + infinitive, recommend / suggest + -ing or that + (should) + base form.

Experts urge doctors to prescribe antibiotics only when absolutely necessary.

6. Impersonal passives — It has been found / shown / suggested that… or X is thought / believed to… — report findings without naming a source. In academic writing, tenses do not usually move back if the finding is still true.

It has been shown that AI tools perform less well on groups that are under-represented in their training data.

ACADEMIC WRITINGReferring to sources — reporting research findings accurately
ACADEMIC WRITING SKILLReferring to sources

In academic writing you must show clearly where information comes from, using phrases such as According to…, X found that… or As X points out,…. Reporting a finding accurately — without exaggerating it, changing its meaning or presenting it as your own idea — is the most effective way to avoid plagiarism.

SOURCE: Smith & Patel (2021): Of 400 patients surveyed, 72% said that a video consultation had fully met their needs.

REPORTED: According to Smith and Patel (2021), almost three-quarters of the patients they surveyed felt that a video consultation had been sufficient.

Read the following text for questions 30-35.

IS GRAFFITI ART OR CRIME?

The term graffiti derives from the Italian graffito meaning ‘scratching’ and can be defined as uninvited marking or writing scratched or applied to objects, built structures and natural features. It is not a new phenomenon: examples can be found on ancient structures around the world, in some cases predating the Greeks and Romans. In such circumstances it has acquired invaluable historical and archaeological significance, providing a social history of life and events at that time. Graffiti is now a problem that has become pervasive, as a result of the availability of cheap and quick means of mark-making.

It is usually considered a priority to remove graffiti as quickly as possible after it appears. This is for several reasons. The first is to prevent ‘copy-cat’ emulation which can occur rapidly once a clean surface is defaced. It may also be of a racist or otherwise offensive nature and many companies and councils have a policy of removing this type of graffiti within an hour or two of it being reported. Also, as paints, glues and inks dry out over time they can become increasingly difficult to remove and are usually best dealt with as soon as possible after the incident. Graffiti can also lead to more serious forms of vandalism and, ultimately, the deterioration of an area, contributing to social decline.

Although graffiti may be regarded as an eyesore, any proposal to remove it from sensitive historic surfaces should be carefully considered: techniques designed for more robust or utilitarian surfaces may result in considerable damage. In the event of graffiti incidents, it is important that the owners of buildings or other structures and their consultants are aware of the approach they should take in dealing with the problem. The police should be informed as there may be other related attacks occurring locally. An incidence pattern can identify possible culprits, as can stylised signatures or nicknames, known as ‘tags’, which may already be familiar to local police. Photographs are useful to record graffiti incidents and may assist the police in bringing a prosecution. Such images are also required for insurance claims and can be helpful in cleaning operatives, allowing them to see the problem area before arriving on site.

There are a variety of methods that are used to remove graffiti. Broadly these divide between chemical and mechanical systems. Chemical preparations are based on dissolving the media; these solvents can range from water to potentially hazardous chemical ‘cocktails’. Mechanical systems such as wire-brushing and grit-blasting attempt to abrade or chip the media from the surface. Care should be taken to comply with health and safety legislation with regard to the protection of both passers-by and any person carrying out the cleaning. Operatives should follow product guidelines in terms of application and removal, and wear the appropriate protective equipment. Measures must be taken to ensure that run-off, aerial mists, drips and splashes do not threaten unprotected members of the public. When examining a graffiti incident it is important to assess the ability of the substrate to withstand the prescribed treatment. If there is any doubt regarding this, then small trial areas should be undertaken to assess the impact of more extensive treatment.

A variety of preventive strategies can be adopted to combat a recurring problem of graffiti at a given site. As no two sites are the same, no one set of protection measures will be suitable for all situations. Each site must be looked at individually. Surveillance systems such as closed-circuit television may also help. In cities and towns around the country, prominently placed cameras have been shown to reduce anti-social behavior of all types including graffiti. Security patrols will also act as a deterrent to prevent recurring attacks. However, the cost of this may be too high for most situations. A physical barriers such as a wall, railings, doors or gates can be introduced to discourage unauthorized access to a vulnerable site. However, consideration has to be given to the impact measures have on the structure being protected. In the worst cases, they can be almost as damaging to the quality of the environment as the graffiti they prevent. In others, they might simply provide a new surface for graffiti.

One of the most significant problems associated with graffiti removal is the need to remove it from surfaces that are repeatedly attacked. Under these circumstances, the repeated removal of graffiti using even the most gentle methods will ultimately cause damage to the surface material. There may be situations where the preventive strategies mentioned above do not work or are not a viable proposition at a given site. Anti-graffiti coatings are usually applied by brush or spray leaving a thin veneer that essentially serves to isolate the graffiti from the surface.

Removal of graffiti from a surface that has been treated in this way is much easier, usually using low-pressure water which reduces the possibility of damage. Depending on the type of barrier selected it may be necessary to reapply the coating after each graffiti removal exercise.

Phrases & Idioms Wordlist

Under the weather: Feeling slightly ill or not as well as usual.

On the mend: Recovering after an illness or injury.

A clean bill of health: An official statement that someone is healthy, or that something is in good condition.

Back on one's feet: Healthy and active again after being ill or having problems.

As fit as a fiddle: In excellent physical health.

Run down: Tired, weak and more likely to become ill, usually because of overwork or stress.

Take a turn for the worse: To suddenly become more ill or a situation becoming much worse.

Out of the woods: No longer in danger or serious difficulty, especially after an illness.

A bitter pill to swallow: An unpleasant fact or situation that is difficult to accept.

Kill or cure: Describing a risky treatment or action that will either solve a problem completely or make it much worse.

Prevention is better than cure: It is easier and wiser to stop a problem happening than to deal with it afterwards.

Just what the doctor ordered: Exactly what is needed to make someone feel better or improve a situation.

Go under the knife: To have a surgical operation.

Burn the candle at both ends: To work or stay active from early morning until late at night, so that you become exhausted.

Have a frog in one's throat: To have difficulty speaking clearly because your throat feels rough or blocked.

SAMPLE ANSWER

Dear Dr Karimova,

Thank you for informing students about the planned changes to the Health Centre's appointment system. I welcome the aim of reducing waiting times, as I have often waited over an hour for a walk-in appointment. However, I must admit that I have some concerns about relying so heavily on video consultations.

Firstly, not all students have a quiet, private place to discuss health problems, particularly those who share rooms in halls of residence. I would therefore suggest providing a few private booths on campus where students can join video calls confidentially.

Secondly, it would be beneficial to keep a small number of same-day appointments for urgent cases, since some illnesses cannot wait for an online booking slot. In addition, clear instructions on using the new system should be sent to international students in several languages.

Thank you for taking the time to consider students' views. I look forward to hearing how the new system develops.

Yours sincerely,

N. Yusupova

QUESTIONS

Answer the questions. Speak for about 30 seconds for each one.

1.  How do you usually look after your health?

2.  Do you prefer to see a doctor in person or online? Why?

3.  When was the last time you visited a doctor or a clinic?

4.  Do you think people in your country take too many medicines?

5.  Would you trust an app to tell you what is wrong with you?

SAMPLE ANSWERS

Do you prefer to see a doctor in person or online? Why?

On the whole, I'd rather see a doctor in person. It's much easier to explain what's wrong when someone can actually examine you. That said, for something simple like renewing a prescription, an online appointment saves a lot of time, so I can see the appeal for busy people.

Do you think people in your country take too many medicines?

To some extent, yes. A lot of people reach for painkillers or antibiotics the moment they feel slightly under the weather, often without asking a doctor first. I think it's partly because medicines are so easy to buy here, but it would be better if people tried rest and fluids first.

Would you trust an app to tell you what is wrong with you?

Only up to a point. I'd happily use one to get a rough idea of what might be wrong, but I wouldn't rely on it completely. Apps can't see the whole picture, so for anything serious I'd definitely want a second opinion from a real doctor.

USEFUL LANGUAGE
Giving a preference:On the whole, I'd rather… / I tend to prefer… because…
Talking about habits:I usually make a point of… / I try to… whenever I can.
Partly agreeing:To some extent, yes. / Only up to a point. / That depends on…
Giving reasons:I think it's partly because… / The main reason is that…
Adding a contrast:That said, … / On the other hand, … / Having said that, …

THE SECRETS OF A LONG LIFE

1 In 1900, a baby born in most European countries could expect to live to around fifty. Today, the same child might reasonably hope to reach eighty or beyond, and in Japan average life expectancy now exceeds eighty-four. This dramatic rise in longevity is one of the great achievements of the modern era, yet it happened so gradually that few people noticed it taking place. Understanding where those extra decades came from tells us a great deal about what we might do to gain a few more.

2 Surprisingly, much of the early progress had little to do with hospitals or advanced medicine. Improvements in sanitation — clean drinking water, proper sewage systems and safer food storage — sharply reduced deaths from infectious diseases such as cholera and typhoid. Because these illnesses killed so many young children, preventing them raised average life expectancy far more than any later treatment for heart disease or cancer. Vaccination programmes and, later, antibiotics continued the trend, turning once-fatal childhood illnesses into rare and manageable events.

3 In the second half of the twentieth century, the focus shifted towards older adults. Medical advances made it possible to prolong the lives of people with conditions that would once have been fatal: blood pressure medication, heart surgery and cancer screening allowed patients to live with illness for years rather than months. Critics point out, however, that adding years to life is not the same as adding life to years. Many people now spend their final decade managing several chronic conditions at once.

4 This distinction led researchers to look for places where people not only live long but also stay healthy. In the early 2000s, a team of scientists identified five regions — Okinawa in Japan, Sardinia in Italy, Nicoya in Costa Rica, Ikaria in Greece and Loma Linda in California — where an unusually high proportion of residents become centenarians. They called these regions 'blue zones', after the blue ink first used to circle them on a map, and began to study what made them different.

5 What do these communities have in common? Remarkably, none of them relies on gyms or fashionable diets. Instead, physical activity is built into everyday life: residents garden, walk to visit neighbours and climb hills to reach their fields, so they rarely lead a sedentary existence. Their diets are largely plant-based, with beans, whole grains and vegetables forming the staple foods, while meat is eaten only occasionally. Many also eat in moderation; Okinawans, for instance, traditionally stop eating when they feel about eighty per cent full.

6 Just as important, it seems, are the social and emotional sides of life. Older people in blue zones typically live close to their families, remain respected members of their communities and have a clear sense of purpose — a reason to get up in the morning. Strong social networks appear to build resilience, helping people cope with stress, illness and loss. Loneliness, by contrast, has been linked to health risks comparable to those of smoking, which suggests that friendship may be as vital to a long life as diet.

7 Not everyone accepts the blue-zone story uncritically. Some researchers argue that birth records in certain regions are unreliable, and that a few supposed centenarians may simply have been younger than they claimed. Others warn that genes play a part that lifestyle cannot fully replace. Even so, the broader lessons — move naturally, eat mostly plants, stay connected — are supported by a large body of evidence. There is no guarantee that these habits will help anyone outlive their parents, but small daily choices may decide how well we spend the years we have.

LANGUAGE DEVELOPMENT - Talking about age and later life

VOCABULARY SKILLVerb + noun collocations

Many verbs combine with a fixed set of nouns when we talk about age, work and family responsibilities — for example lead an active lifestyle, take early retirement or shoulder the burden of caring for a relative. Learning these combinations as complete chunks makes your speaking and writing sound more natural and precise, and helps you avoid unnatural choices such as make a pension or do a lifestyle.

takeearly retirement, responsibility for someone

WHO WILL CARE FOR AN AGEING WORLD?

1. For most of human history, societies were shaped like pyramids: a broad base of children and young adults supported a narrow peak of older people. That shape is now changing rapidly. As people live longer and families have fewer children, the demographic pyramid in many countries is turning into something closer to a column. By 2050, according to United Nations estimates, one in six people worldwide will be over sixty-five, and in parts of Europe and East Asia the figure will be closer to one in three. This transformation raises difficult questions about money, work and care.

2. The most immediate concern is pensions. Most state pension systems were designed on a simple principle: today's workers pay for today's retirees. When there were five or six workers for every pensioner, this arrangement worked well. Now that the ratio is falling towards two to one in some countries, it is placing considerable strain on public finances. Governments face an uncomfortable choice between raising taxes on a shrinking working population, reducing pension payments, or asking people to work for longer. None of these options is popular, and attempts to introduce them have led to strikes and protests in several countries.

3. Increasingly, the third option is the one being chosen. Many countries have gradually raised the official retirement age, and a growing number of people choose to postpone retirement voluntarily. Supporters argue that this makes sense: people are healthier at sixty-five than their grandparents were, and keeping experienced employees in the workforce helps companies retain valuable knowledge. Critics, however, point out that not every job can be done at seventy. A university lecturer may happily continue teaching, whereas a builder or a nurse working night shifts may simply be physically unable to carry on.

4. Pensions and work are only part of the picture. As people live longer, the need for long-term care rises too. In much of Western Europe and North America, this care is increasingly provided by professional services such as nursing homes, which are expensive and often short of staff. Where such services are unavailable or unaffordable, the burden usually falls on families, and in particular on middle-aged women, who may find themselves looking after their own children and their elderly parents at the same time — a situation often described as being part of the 'sandwich generation'.

5. In Uzbekistan, as in much of Central Asia, the picture looks rather different. Multigenerational households, in which grandparents, parents and children live under one roof, remain common, and it is traditionally the youngest son and his wife who stay in the family home to look after his parents. These intergenerational arrangements bring clear benefits: older people are rarely isolated, and grandparents play a central role in raising grandchildren, passing on language, customs and values. Respect for elders, shown in everyday gestures and in the advice sought from the oqsoqol of the mahalla, helps to strengthen social cohesion in the wider community.

6. Such traditions are not immune to change. Urbanisation and migration for work mean that more young families now live in apartments far from their parents, and the extended household is less universal than it once was. Nevertheless, the multigenerational model offers lessons that other societies are beginning to recognise. The unpaid contribution of older people — caring for grandchildren, volunteering, advising younger relatives — is often undervalued because it does not appear in economic statistics. If ageing societies are to thrive, they may need to see older citizens less as a cost to be managed and more as a resource to be valued.

GRAMMAR FOR WRITING
GRAMMARConcession and contrast

Academic writers rarely present only one side of an issue. Language of concession allows them to accept that an opposing fact or argument is true, while still showing that their main point is stronger. Language of contrast shows how two facts or situations differ.

The rules below explain how to use the most common expressions of concession and contrast, and which grammatical structures follow them.

1. Use although / even though + a full clause (subject + verb). Even though is more emphatic. The clause can come first (followed by a comma) or second.

Although life expectancy has risen, many people spend their final years in poor health.

2. Use despite / in spite of + a noun, a pronoun or an -ing form — never a full clause. To add a clause, use despite the fact that.

Despite living alone, my great-aunt rarely feels lonely. / In spite of the fact that she lives alone, she rarely feels lonely.

3. Use whereas / while + clause to contrast two different facts or situations, usually within one sentence.

Okinawans eat mainly vegetables, whereas many Western diets are high in red meat.

4. Use however / nevertheless / nonetheless to link two separate sentences. They usually come at the start of the second sentence, followed by a comma. Nevertheless means 'despite what has just been said'.

Raising the pension age is deeply unpopular. Nevertheless, many governments see no realistic alternative.

5. Use admittedly / it is true that / granted to concede a point, then follow it with but / however / even so to return to your main argument.

Admittedly, some older workers are slower to adopt new technology. However, they often bring decades of valuable experience.

6. Use even so / all the same at the start of a sentence to introduce a surprising contrast with what has just been said.

The village has no hospital and few doctors. Even so, its residents are among the healthiest in the country.

ACADEMIC WRITINGCounter-arguments and refutation — answering the other side
ACADEMIC WRITING SKILLCounter-arguments and refutation

A persuasive argument becomes stronger, not weaker, when the writer acknowledges what opponents believe. First present the opposing view fairly (Opponents argue that… / It is sometimes claimed that…), then refute it by showing its weakness (However, this overlooks… / This argument fails to take into account… / While this may be true, …). The refutation should be supported by a reason, a fact or an example rather than a simple denial.

COUNTER-ARGUMENT: Opponents argue that raising the retirement age is unfair to people in physically demanding jobs.

REFUTATION: However, this overlooks the fact that flexible schemes could allow such workers to move into lighter roles or reduce their hours, rather than leave work altogether.

I. Family reunions can be a joyous occasion and an opportunity to meet new family members as well. Our parents have aunts, uncles and cousins that we may only meet once or twice in life. Often, though, meeting an extended family member can be like meeting a complete stranger. You’re not even sure you will like them, and the whole affair can feel a bit odd or uncomfortable.

II. Traditionally, the mother is the primary caregiver to an infant child. She takes time off work and stays at home to provide round-the-clock attention during the child’s early years. But recently, more and more men are taking paternity leave from work to stay at home with their new-borns. Mothers find it a welcome trend, as caring for an infant can be exhausting work.

III. While it’s true that kids must carry out their responsibilities just as adults do, sometimes Mum and Dad have to be a bit crafty to make it happen. They have to offer a little reward for a job well done. It may not be good practice to do it all the time, but if they promise a trip to the cinema, for example, the kids will be more likely to clean their rooms.

IV. Many families live far away from one another these days. They may have moved across the country, or even to the other side of the world. It’s especially hard for parents to see their children do this, either for work or for adventure. So when special occasions come round, especially the holiday seasons, Mum and Dad are so grateful when their sons and daughters return home.

V. Sometimes a household is nothing but chaos for days on end. This is especially true when kids reach their adolescent phase, and you have a couple of teenagers who compete over every little thing in life. No matter how often parents attempt to stop two kids from fighting each other, nothing seems to work. They just have to wait until one of them moves away to university!

VI. In most families, parents have to constantly remind their children of their responsibilities. But there are times when kids can be especially useful round the house of their own will. They also understand those times when Mum or Dad isn’t feeling well, and maybe it would be nice if they made dinner for a change or did a little extra tidying up in the living room.

Phrases & Idioms Wordlist

Over the hill: Past one's best; considered too old for something (often used humorously).

Long in the tooth: Old, especially too old for a particular activity or job.

Young at heart: Feeling and behaving in a youthful, energetic way despite being old.

Age is just a number: A person's age need not limit what they can do or enjoy.

Getting on (in years): Becoming old.

Live to a ripe old age: To live until one is very old.

In one's prime: At the period of life when one is strongest, healthiest or most successful.

Act one's age: To behave in a way that is suitable for someone of one's age, especially more maturely.

Turn back the clock: To return to an earlier time, or to try to make things as they were in the past.

Old habits die hard: It is very difficult to stop doing something you have done for a long time.

Time flies: Time seems to pass very quickly.

One's twilight years: The last part of a person's life.

A senior moment: A short lapse of memory, humorously linked to getting older.

Set in one's ways: Unwilling to change one's habits or opinions, often because of age.

The generation gap: The differences in attitudes, values and tastes between younger and older people.

THE TASK

You are writing an essay for an academic audience. Write 180–200 words.

In many countries, people are now expected to work until they are sixty-five or even older. Some people think this is a positive development, while others believe it is unfair. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

PARAGRAPH PLAN

Introductionparaphrase the question + state your position briefly
Body paragraph 1arguments in favour of working longer, with reasons and examples
Body paragraph 2the opposing view (counter-argument) + your refutation
Conclusionsummarise both views and restate your opinion in new words

RULES for Part 2 (essay)

☐  Answer ALL parts of the question — discuss both views AND give your own opinion.

☐  Write 180–200 words in four clear paragraphs: introduction, two body paragraphs and a conclusion.

☐  State your position in the introduction and keep it consistent throughout the essay.

☐  Include at least one counter-argument and refute it with a reason or an example.

☐  Use a formal, academic register: no contractions, no slang, and avoid 'I think' in every sentence.

☐  Show a range of grammar, including concession and contrast (although, despite, whereas, nevertheless).

SAMPLE ANSWER

In many countries, the official retirement age has risen to sixty-five or beyond, and people are increasingly expected to remain in work for longer. While some welcome this trend, others regard it as deeply unfair.

Those in favour point out that people today are considerably healthier than previous generations were at the same age, so many are perfectly capable of continuing to work. Keeping experienced employees in the workforce also allows companies to benefit from their knowledge, and it reduces the pressure on pension systems that are already struggling to cope.

Opponents argue that a higher retirement age punishes people in physically demanding jobs, who may be exhausted long before they reach sixty-five. Admittedly, this is a serious concern. However, it overlooks the possibility of flexible schemes, which could allow such workers to move into lighter roles or reduce their hours gradually rather than stop altogether.

In my view, working longer is a sensible response to longer lives, provided that it is not imposed in the same way on everyone. Although no system will satisfy every worker, a flexible approach would protect both public finances and the dignity of older people.

PART 2 PRACTICE — now you try

Some people believe that elderly parents should live with their adult children, while others think they are better cared for in professional care homes. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

SPEAKING PART 3
STATEMENT

Elderly people should live with their families rather than in care homes.

Discuss both sides of the statement and give your own opinion. Use the points below to help you.

FORAGAINST
older people feel loved and are rarely lonelyfamilies may lack the medical skills needed
grandparents help raise children and pass on traditionscarers, often women, can become exhausted
it is cheaper than paying for professional caresmall city apartments may not have enough space
SAMPLE ANSWER

I'd say I largely agree with this statement, although I can see that it isn't the right solution for every family.

The strongest argument in favour is emotional. There's no doubt that older people who live with their children and grandchildren feel valued and are far less likely to suffer from loneliness, which, as we know, can seriously damage health. On top of that, grandparents play a huge role in bringing up children — in my own family, my grandmother taught us our first songs and recipes. It's also worth mentioning that family care is usually much cheaper than a care home.

Having said that, there are some convincing arguments on the other side. Admittedly, a family can't always provide the medical care that someone with a serious illness needs, and the person who does most of the caring — usually a daughter or daughter-in-law — can become completely exhausted. What's more, many young couples in cities now live in small apartments, so there simply isn't enough room.

All things considered, I think living with the family is the best option in most cases, because it benefits every generation. Nevertheless, I believe professional care should be available, and families shouldn't feel ashamed of using it when an elderly relative's needs become too great for them to manage at home.

USEFUL LANGUAGE
Giving your overall view:I largely agree with… / I'm not entirely convinced that…
Presenting arguments for:The strongest argument in favour is… / There's no doubt that…
Adding points:On top of that, … / What's more, … / It's also worth mentioning that…
Moving to the other side:Having said that, … / On the other hand, … / Admittedly, …
Giving examples:In my own family, … / Take my grandparents, for instance…
Concluding:All things considered, … / On balance, I'd say… / Nevertheless, I believe…
